name: Robert Reich
role: US Secretary of Labor (1993–1997), Berkeley professor and commentator
summary: Reich is an American economist and Berkeley professor who served as Labor Secretary under Bill Clinton. He argues that market rules are political choices and have been rewritten for the wealthy, and he advocates progressive taxation, universal Medicare, stronger unions, antitrust and campaign finance reform to rebuild a broad middle class.

notes: Answers rest on Reich's five local books (Aftershock, Beyond Outrage, Saving Capitalism, The Common Good, Supercapitalism) plus two NPR transcripts (2011 public unions, 2013 minimum wage). Themes searched: economy, taxes, labor, health care, money in politics, trade, immigration, nationalism, religion, civil liberties, separation of powers, federalism, race and voting rights, Marxism. Passages where Reich describes a demagogue's platform (e.g. tariffs, leaving the UN, a freeze on immigration in Aftershock) were treated as his criticism, not his position, and left unanswered where he gave no view of his own. Nothing found on secession, minority languages, monarchy, military alliances or religion in law; those stay null. The uncertainty rule passes at 46 known answers.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Aftershock's reform agenda ("Medicare for all") says the next stage after the 2010 law should let everyone sign up for Medicare; Beyond Outrage repeats it as "Fight for Medicare for All".

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Supercapitalism calls for raising the minimum wage high enough to give working people a true living wage, and on NPR he said full-time workers should not be in poverty.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Beyond Outrage demands a 70 percent rate on income over $1 million and Aftershock proposes 55, 50 and 40 percent top brackets, so the rich pay a much larger share.

unions-good.rationale: Saving Capitalism names the demise of unions as a driving force behind the shrinking middle class and wants workers in low-wage industries able to form unions by majority vote to gain bargaining leverage over wages and benefits.

property-fundamental.rationale: Saving Capitalism argues property is defined by legislatures and courts, changes over time, and is not a fixed natural right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Saving Capitalism's agenda calls for enforcement resources and fines large enough to deter corporate lawbreaking, a ban on forced arbitration and restored Glass-Steagall limits.

state-harmful.rationale: He holds that government creates and enforces the rules that make markets function and calls for a larger public role, which contradicts abolishing the state.

decide-locally.rationale: The Common Good says Americans believe in federalism, giving states and localities significant responsibilities.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Aftershock criticises the demagogues' platform of a freeze on legal immigration and notes that Americans are mostly a nation of immigrants.

nation-first.rationale: The Common Good says we are not in a zero-sum game with the rest of the world, that our common good is bound up with the planet's, and criticises the Trump administration for abandoning that stance.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Aftershock proposes a rising carbon tax, and Beyond Outrage lists reversing climate change as a worthy fight.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Saving Capitalism approves Paine's proposal of a tax on inherited land to fund a basic minimum and wants rules that stop great wealth compounding for heirs, and criticises the cut estate tax.

basic-income.rationale: Saving Capitalism (chapter "When Robots Take Over") proposes a minimum guaranteed income for all citizens, financed by reverting breakthrough-technology wealth to the public, though as one option among alternatives.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Common Good endorses democracy based on consent of the governed with checks and balances, and warns against open societies turning closed and autocratic.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Common Good rejects the idea that national identity rests on the whiteness of our skin or uniformity of ethnicity; he says it is the ideals Americans share.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Saving Capitalism says laws could require that employees be represented on corporate boards with voting rights proportional to their stakes, citing German co-determination.

school-vouchers.rationale: Aftershock proposes replacing public school spending with vouchers inversely related to family income, usable at any school meeting minimum standards.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Beyond Outrage says there is no problem borrowing to invest in education and infrastructure and that low borrowing costs make now the ideal time; Aftershock likewise urges demand-boosting measures.

night-watchman-state.rationale: His agenda calls for public health insurance, free public college, public goods and strong enforcement, so government goes well beyond protecting people from violence.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Saving Capitalism's money-in-politics agenda would ban gerrymandered districts that suppress minority votes and voting restrictions that burden minorities disproportionately.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Common Good says Americans are committed to the Constitution, the rule of law and democracy based on the consent of the governed, and presents this as the shared ideal he holds.

separated-powers.rationale: The Common Good lists the citizen commitments Reich shares: an independent judiciary, separation of powers among executive, legislature and courts, and checks and balances among them.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The Common Good says the core of American identity is shared ideals, not uniformity of ethnicity, and Aftershock condemns demagogues who attack new immigrants in a nation of immigrants.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Common Good lists commitment to freedom of speech and a free and independent press among the principles Americans share, which he endorses.

ban-cartels.rationale: Saving Capitalism wants antitrust used against collusion and insurers no longer exempt, so they could not fix prices or allocate markets.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Saving Capitalism's agenda would require all trade-agreement partners to set minimum wages equal to half their median wage.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Saving Capitalism says that, contrary to Marx, nothing about capitalism leads inexorably to mounting insecurity and inequality, and its rules can be rewritten to work for the many.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Common Good says citizens are committed to the Bill of Rights and an independent judiciary; it does not discuss how hard it should be to amend.

corporate-influence.rationale: Beyond Outrage's central argument is that corporate lobbying and campaign money from corporations and Wall Street distort political decisions and make politicians dependent on their patrons.

religious-nation.rationale: The Common Good says some think we are connected by adherence to Christianity but he believes we are bound together by shared ideals and principles instead.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Beyond Outrage calls it good to push for gay rights.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Common Good says citizens are committed to free speech, a free press and bound as political equals to accept outcomes; it warns that demagogues push societies toward closed and autocratic rule.

social-market-economy.rationale: He argues for reforming capitalism with stronger safety nets, unions and public goods rather than abolishing the market, as in Saving Capitalism and Aftershock.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Beyond Outrage quotes Brandeis that we can have democracy or concentrated wealth but not both, and Aftershock names the political threat of extreme inequality.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Saving Capitalism criticises the growing non-working rich and wants capital gains taxed like wages.

free-public-college.rationale: Aftershock's agenda says tuition should be free at all public colleges and universities, financed by a share of graduates' later earnings.

arms-reduction.rationale: Beyond Outrage says hundreds of billions could be cut from the Pentagon, ending obsolete weapons and cutting strategic nuclear forces, without jeopardizing security.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Saving Capitalism wants low-wage workers able to unionize to bargain over wages and benefits, but does not say bargaining alone should set wages.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Aftershock says the Earned Income Tax Credit should be expanded and extended upward, and Common Good lists bigger wage subsidies through the EITC among needed measures.

sacred-nation.rationale: The Common Good rejects a 'we're better than anyone else' nationalism as the core of American identity and warns of leaders inciting rabid nationalism.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Beyond Outrage condemns subsidies, bailouts, loan guarantees and other corporate welfare for the well-connected, and Saving Capitalism wants upward pre-distributions in market rules ended.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Beyond Outrage's agenda proposes a one-half of 1 percent tax on all financial transactions to slow speculation and raise revenue.

wages-fall-to-bare-minimum.rationale: Saving Capitalism rejects the Marxian claim of an inexorable slide, arguing wage levels depend on rules that can be changed, such as bargaining power and the minimum wage.

human-caused-global-warming.rationale: Saving Capitalism treats an "expert" funded by Koch Industries asserting that humans have no part in climate change as an example of a claim the public needs funding disclosure to weigh.

shut-down-tax-havens.rationale: Aftershock asks why America did not attack overseas tax havens, and Beyond Outrage's corporate pledge would have firms promise not to shift money to offshore havens.

limit-campaign-donations.rationale: Beyond Outrage's agenda calls for stricter limits on campaign contributions, public matching financing and a constitutional amendment to reverse Citizens United.
